clinicalPearls: Occurs days to a couple of weeks after transfusion as an anamnestic alloantibody response boosts a previously undetectable red-cell antibody
Typical picture is an unexpected fall or failure to sustain the haemoglobin, mild jaundice and a low-grade fever after apparently uneventful transfusion
Commonly involves antibodies of the Rh, Kidd, Duffy and Kell systems whose titres had waned below detection at pretransfusion testing
Haemolysis is largely extravascular, so it is usually less dramatic than an acute intravascular reaction
The direct antiglobulin test becomes positive and a newly identified alloantibody appears on repeat screening
Management is largely supportive, with monitoring of haemoglobin and renal function and provision of antigen-negative blood for future transfusion
Sickle cell disease patients are particularly vulnerable and may develop hyperhaemolysis with a haemoglobin lower than before transfusion
reference.pathophysiology: A delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction reflects an anamnestic (secondary) immune response. A patient previously alloimmunised by transfusion or pregnancy carries an antibody whose level has fallen below the threshold of pretransfusion detection, so nominally compatible antigen-positive cells are transfused. Re-exposure rapidly boosts antibody production over the following days, and the antibodies coat the transfused cells, which are then cleared largely by the mononuclear phagocyte system in the spleen and liver. The result is extravascular haemolysis with a delayed, often modest fall in haemoglobin, a rise in bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase, and conversion of the direct antiglobulin test to positive as the new antibody appears.
additionalDifferentials: Ongoing bleeding causing a falling haemoglobin
Hyperhaemolysis syndrome in sickle cell disease
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test, which characteristically becomes positive after transfusion
Repeat antibody screen and identification to detect a newly emerged alloantibody
Haemolysis markers including lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin and reticulocytes
Blood film for spherocytes and evidence of haemolysis
Serial haemoglobin to document the delayed fall or failure to increment
Renal function monitoring for the less common cases with significant haemolysis
redFlags: Unexplained falling haemoglobin with jaundice several days after transfusion
Marked haemolysis with haemoglobinuria and renal impairment
A post-transfusion haemoglobin lower than baseline suggesting hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease
Rapidly rising antibody titre with brisk red-cell destruction
reference.prognosis: Most reactions are mild and self-limiting as the transfused cells are cleared, but significant haemolysis can occur, and in sickle cell disease hyperhaemolysis may be life-threatening and worsened by further transfusion.
pitfalls: Attributing the falling haemoglobin to bleeding and giving more antigen-positive blood
Overlooking a previously identified alloantibody that has since become undetectable
Missing hyperhaemolysis in sickle cell disease, where further transfusion can be harmful
Failing to flag the new antibody so that future units are appropriately antigen-negative
management: Supportive management is the mainstay, as extravascular haemolysis is usually modest and self-limiting as the transfused cells are cleared
Supply antigen-negative, compatible red cells for any subsequent transfusion, matched to the newly detected alloantibody
Serial haemoglobin and haemolysis markers (lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin, bilirubin, reticulocytes) to monitor the delayed fall or failure to increment
Monitor renal function and maintain hydration in the less common cases with significant haemolysis
Document the alloantibody and issue a patient alert card to prevent recurrence at future transfusion
Investigate and report the reaction through the transfusion laboratory with direct antiglobulin test and repeat antibody identification

In sickle cell disease be alert to potentially life-threatening hyperhaemolysis, avoid further transfusion where possible and escalate with immunosuppression such as corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin
